strengths: The paper addresses an important Text-to-SQL problem and proposes a coherent three-stage system: schema grounding, interactive multi-turn SQL generation, and learned trajectory validation.

The empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks, especially 77.84% EX on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, with useful ablations showing gains from grounding, verification, multiple candidates, and interaction turns.
The method is practically motivated: live database feedback, execution-based rewards, and candidate reranking are well aligned with real Text-to-SQL failure modes.
The appendix includes prompts, dataset construction details, and some hyperparameters, and the ethics statement acknowledges risks from incorrect queries.
weaknesses: The central technical novelty is limited. The framework combines known ingredients: ReAct-style tool use, GRPO/RL fine-tuning, schema pruning, best-of-N sampling, and generative verification. The paper does not clearly establish what is algorithmically new beyond this integration.

The soundness of the SOTA claims is weakened by incomplete experimental controls. Comparisons appear to mix different inference budgets, training data, model sizes, and closed/open-source systems, and there is no cost/latency/compute-normalized comparison despite the method relying on multiple interactive rollouts and reranking.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for an ICML main-track claim. The code URL is blank, models are only promised after publication, and key details are missing or underspecified, including number of GPUs, training steps, GRPO group size, KL settings, rollout limits, max tokens, seeds, exact candidate counts used in main results, and benchmark submission/evaluation protocols.

The training/evaluation setup raises possible leakage or overfitting concerns that are not fully addressed. BIRD-dev is the main in-domain evaluation and appears to guide many design choices; the paper does not report a held-out BIRD test result or confidence intervals. The verifier training uses execution labels from generated trajectories, but the construction and handling of ground-truth SQL suggestions for all-negative cases is not sufficiently analyzed.

Several ablations are suggestive but not decisive. The paper lacks comparisons against prompt-only ReAct with the same rollout budget, RL generator without multi-turn database feedback, verifier trained without trajectory observations, or stronger open-source rerankers under matched compute.

The presentation has noticeable issues that reduce confidence. The manuscript contains typos and formatting inconsistencies, and Figure 5 appears internally inconsistent: the described order of corrections does not match the displayed observations/thoughts, and the final SQL contains quoting/column syntax issues that may be invalid SQLite.

The limitations discussion is very thin. It does not quantify failure modes, runtime/database interaction cost, security concerns from executing generated SQL, sensitivity to schema size, or risks from using execution accuracy when semantically wrong queries can coincidentally match results.

strengths: The paper targets an important and active problem: robust text-to-SQL over complex schemas with execution feedback. The decomposition into grounding, interactive generation, and validation is sensible and aligns with practical failure modes in SQL agents.

The reported empirical numbers are strong: 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK, with ablations suggesting that grounding, RL-trained generation, and learned validation each contribute.

The paper includes useful appendices with prompt templates, some hyperparameters, grounding precision/recall, turn-budget ablations, and selection-method comparisons. The ethics statement acknowledges risks from incorrect generated queries.
weaknesses: The central claims are not sufficiently supported for acceptance. The method is a combination of known components: schema pruning, ReAct-style SQL execution, GRPO/RL fine-tuning, best-of-N sampling, and a learned verifier. The paper does not clearly isolate what is technically new beyond assembling these ingredients, and the novelty over closely related text-to-SQL agents and RL SQL systems is underargued.

Reproducibility is weak despite a reproducibility statement. The abstract says code is available but gives no URL. Critical details are missing or underspecified: number of GPUs/training steps, optimizer settings for RL, KL coefficients, group size, rollout limits, exact reward computation, validation data construction, inference cost, stopping criteria, database execution sandbox, and how official/hidden Spider test results were obtained.

There are internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence in the evidence. The validation agent is described as scoring full trajectories and averaging stochastic Yes-token probabilities, but the appendix prompt only shows the question and proposed solution, not the full trajectory or execution observations. The validation training data is said to include the final execution result, which may leak a very strong correctness signal during training unless carefully controlled; this is not analyzed.

The example trajectory in Figure 5 appears out of order and contains SQL errors/formatting mistakes. It first reports an error for table `fprm`, then says the query executed successfully and returned empty before showing the corrected table, and later produces SQL with an unquoted column name containing spaces. This casts doubt on the claimed self-correction demonstration and on the care of the system description.

The experimental comparison is not fully fair or transparent. Baselines mix closed-source systems, base models, and trained systems with different training data and inference budgets. The paper does not report compute-normalized or sample-normalized comparisons, although MARS-SQL uses multiple rollouts, execution feedback, grounding, and reranking. Claims of state of the art are therefore stronger than the evidence warrants.

Ablations are helpful but incomplete. There is no clean comparison to a non-RL multi-turn generator with the same prompts and rollouts, no analysis of failure cases, no statistical uncertainty, no per-query-complexity breakdown, and no measurement of execution/query cost. The paper also does not separate gains from schema pruning, extra test-time sampling, verifier training, and access to execution observations as cleanly as needed.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard. There are many typos and formatting problems, including `Obeservation`, missing spaces around MARS-SQL, malformed table text, `Unkonwn`, inconsistent tag casing, and an incomplete code-availability line. Several claims are phrased too broadly, such as saying capabilities are absent in existing systems, without adequate support.

Limitations are not adequately discussed. The paper lacks a substantive limitations section addressing execution-safety risks, dependence on benchmark-specific execution rewards, verifier overfitting, cost/latency from many rollouts, brittleness to noisy schemas or SQL dialects, and the risk of selecting spurious SQL queries that match execution results but are semantically wrong.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving text-to-SQL reliability on complex schemas through interactive database feedback rather than one-shot generation. The proposed decomposition into grounding, multi-turn generation, and validation is well motivated for this setting.

Empirical results are strong. MARS-SQL reports 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and 78.13% on Spider-DK with a 7B backbone, comparing favorably to both open-source trained systems and several closed-source multi-agent frameworks.

The ablations are meaningful and support the main design choices. Removing the verifier or grounder substantially reduces performance, self-consistency is weaker than the learned generative verifier, and the interaction-turn studies show that multi-turn RL improves both greedy and best-of-N behavior.

The methodology is technically plausible and reasonably detailed: the paper specifies the MDP formulation, GRPO objectives, reward design, agent prompts, training data construction, and core hyperparameters. The grounding precision/recall appendix is especially helpful for understanding where gains come from.

The work has practical significance: a learned open-source-style agentic pipeline that can interact with databases and select among trajectories is useful for real deployments where schema grounding, execution feedback, and reranking all matter.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The abstract says code is available but provides no URL, while the reproducibility statement only commits to releasing code and models upon publication. Several important implementation details remain underspecified, including exact compute budget, number of GPUs/training duration, full decoding parameters for all reported results, checkpoint selection, and execution sandbox details.

The comparison to prior systems is somewhat difficult to interpret. Baselines differ in model size, training data, access to proprietary models, use of Spider/BIRD data, and possibly inference budget. The paper would be stronger with a controlled comparison under equal rollout counts, equal base model, and equal verifier budget.

The validation setup raises some concerns. The verifier is trained from generator outputs labeled by execution results, and for questions with only flawed trajectories the authors add the ground-truth SQL as a suggestion. This may be reasonable for training, but the paper should more carefully analyze whether this creates distribution artifacts, overfits to benchmark-style gold queries, or inflates verifier performance on related evaluation distributions.

The claims of state-of-the-art performance are not fully settled because the strongest number on BIRD is on the development set rather than a hidden test set, and the paper does not report statistical uncertainty or significance across sampling seeds. Given that the method relies heavily on stochastic candidate generation and reranking, variance analysis is important.

The cost and latency tradeoffs are underreported. The method generates multiple multi-turn trajectories and then runs a validation agent, so practical utility depends on query executions, tokens, wall-clock time, and database load. The paper reports accuracy but not enough efficiency data to assess deployment viability.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence. There are typos and formatting problems throughout, the abstract has an unfinished code-availability sentence, Table 14 contains 'Unkonwn', and the appendix example appears out of order and includes malformed SQL/quoting. These are fixable, but they matter for a systems-oriented paper where exact prompts and examples are part of the method.

The novelty is useful but mostly compositional: schema grounding, ReAct-style tool interaction, GRPO, best-of-N sampling, and generative verification are all established ingredients. The paper’s main originality is their integration and text-to-SQL-specific training recipe rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

strengths: The paper tackles an important Text-to-SQL problem and proposes a coherent three-role agentic workflow: schema grounding, interactive SQL generation, and trajectory validation. This decomposition is well motivated for large, noisy database schemas.

The empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks: 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, with useful ablations showing that the verifier, schema grounder, and interactive turns each contribute some gain.

The appendices include unusually detailed efficiency and deployment analysis, including latency, token cost, VRAM, training time, and adjustable cost-accuracy tradeoffs. This improves practical interpretability of the system.
The paper attempts to separate architectural gains from parameter count and test-time compute through parameter-matched ensembles, generator scaling, and equal-latency self-consistency comparisons.
weaknesses: The central claim that interactive RL is the main driver is only partially supported. The controlled isolation table attributes a much larger gain to generative verification/reranking (+8.54%) than to RL interactive reasoning (+2.89%), yet the narrative emphasizes the learned ReAct policy as the core contribution.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled or convincing. The single shared-model baselines are SFT-only while MARS-SQL uses role-specific RL/SFT plus reranking; closed-source and open-source baselines differ in training data, inference budget, and candidate generation; and the claimed SOTA status relies mainly on BIRD-dev rather than a hidden/test evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many hyperparameters. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank, and important implementation details are underspecified, including exact reward/evaluation scripts, SQL execution matching, candidate filtering, verifier training labels, and how official Spider-test results were obtained.

The validation agent is not described consistently. The text claims it evaluates against full database schema/context, but the shown prompt contains only the question, external knowledge, and proposed solution. It is unclear whether schema, execution observations, or full trajectories are actually provided at inference.

There are presentation and consistency problems that reduce confidence. For example, the qualitative Figure 6 appears internally reordered: the agent discusses an empty result before the shown empty-result query, then later says it made the table-name correction after already using the corrected table. The final SQL in that example also appears syntactically invalid due to unescaped column names with spaces/parentheses.

Some efficiency claims are speculative or weakly justified, such as the estimate that SFT would require 15M synthetic examples and 3-4 months to match performance. These should not be treated as evidence without a clearer scaling experiment.

Limitations and ethics are present but shallow. The paper acknowledges deployment cost, but gives little discussion of risks from erroneous SQL execution in high-stakes databases, privacy/security concerns of autonomous database access, or safeguards beyond validation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving reliability of Text-to-SQL systems through execution feedback, schema grounding, and candidate verification. The high-level decomposition into grounding, interactive generation, and validation is sensible for complex database tasks.

The manuscript reports extensive empirical results, including main comparisons on BIRD-dev, Spider, and Spider-DK; component ablations; interaction-turn studies; verifier comparisons; and latency/VRAM/token-cost analyses. These are the right kinds of analyses for a multi-agent inference framework.

The reported headline numbers are strong, especially 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev and 89.75% on Spider-test, and the ablations suggest that the verifier and multi-turn generator may be useful components.
The paper is generally readable and includes prompts, hyperparameters, training data construction details, and an explicit discussion of deployment cost and total parameter footprint.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not sufficiently trustworthy as presented. The paper claims code is available, but the link is blank, and there is no artifact, checkpoint, evaluation script, or exact reproduction path. Given the complexity of a three-agent RL/SFT pipeline, this is a major reproducibility failure.

The main comparisons mix heterogeneous systems, training sets, model sizes, inference budgets, and possibly evaluation protocols. Some baselines are closed-source or proprietary, while others are open-source models trained under different data regimes. The paper repeatedly claims state-of-the-art performance, but does not establish a controlled or verifiable leaderboard comparison.

Several decisive claims are overextended relative to the evidence. For example, the statement that SFT would require 15M synthetic examples and 3-4 months of training is described as a conservative scaling-law estimate but no scaling experiment or derivation is provided. Similarly, the system-optimized latency estimates are conceptual rather than measured.

The methodology is not very original at the algorithmic level. The system combines familiar ingredients: schema linking, ReAct-style SQL execution, GRPO with execution rewards, best-of-N sampling, and generative verification/reranking. The contribution is mainly an engineering workflow, but the paper presents it with stronger novelty language than is justified.

The ablations do not fully isolate the effects needed to support the paper’s claims. The largest gain appears to come from validation/reranking and best-of-N sampling, but the paper does not sufficiently compare against equally trained or equally budgeted rerankers and single-agent RL baselines under matched data and implementation conditions.

The validation agent raises potential evaluation leakage and overfitting concerns. It is trained on trajectories generated from filtered BIRD training examples, but the paper does not provide enough detail on negative construction, execution-equivalence labeling, schema overlap, or whether the verifier learns benchmark-specific artifacts rather than general SQL correctness.

The presentation contains concerning inconsistencies and polish issues: missing code URL, typos such as 'baesd' and 'detaile', inconsistent notation, references to Appendix C.1 for prompts that actually appear later, and awkward or possibly erroneous benchmark names and model names such as GPT-5.2. These issues reduce confidence in the care of the experimental report.

The limitations and ethics discussion is shallow. The paper acknowledges inference cost, but gives little treatment of failure modes, unsafe database use, privacy/security risks from autonomous query execution, or the consequences of confidently returning incorrect SQL results in high-stakes settings.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and active problem, Text-to-SQL over realistic databases, and the proposed decomposition into grounding, interactive generation, and validation is well motivated by concrete failure modes: schema distractors, multi-step logical errors, and incorrect-but-executable SQL.

The empirical results are strong. MARS-SQL reports 77.84% execution accuracy on BIRD-dev, 89.75% on Spider-test, and competitive Spider-DK/SParC transfer, with consistent gains over the Qwen base model, open-source Text-to-SQL systems, and several agentic baselines.

The ablation package is unusually thorough. The paper studies component removal, controlled isolation of schema pruning/RL interaction/reranking, turn limits, Best-of-N behavior, selection methods, grounding recall/precision, parameter scaling, and latency/cost tradeoffs. These analyses make the central claims more credible than a headline benchmark table alone would.

The core evidence supports the claim that the gains are not only from more sampling or more parameters. In particular, the RL generator improves greedy accuracy, the verifier improves over self-consistency and LLM-as-judge baselines, and the 21B ensemble/scaled-generator comparisons suggest role specialization matters.

The paper is reasonably transparent about practical costs: it reports total inference footprint, token usage, latency, VRAM under different deployment assumptions, and lower-cost operating points. The limitations discussion around the 3-agent/21B footprint is honest rather than hidden.

Reproducibility is better than average for this type of systems paper: prompts, training data construction, major hyperparameters, hardware, and training times are described, and the impact statement/LLM-use statement are included.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental rather than fundamental: the system combines known ingredients, including ReAct-style interaction, GRPO, schema linking, Best-of-N sampling, and generative verification. The contribution is mainly an effective integration and training recipe, not a new algorithmic primitive.

Some reproducibility details remain underspecified despite the extensive appendix. The paper does not provide a visible code URL in the abstract, and key implementation choices such as exact KL coefficient, clipping epsilon, rollout termination/parsing rules, maximum token lengths, random seeds, database execution sandbox details, and variance across runs are not fully reported.

The strongest benchmark claims rely partly on heterogeneous comparisons to systems with different model access, train sets, inference budgets, and evaluation protocols. The paper does add normalized-budget analyses, but a fully controlled reimplementation of the most relevant recent Text-to-SQL RL/agent baselines would make the state-of-the-art claim more decisive.

The validation-agent training pipeline may introduce subtle dependencies on benchmark-specific execution behavior. The verifier is trained using generated trajectories and execution correctness from BIRD, and in some cases ground-truth SQL is added when only flawed trajectories are available. This is reasonable, but the paper should more clearly discuss whether this biases the verifier toward benchmark artifacts or execution-equivalence shortcuts.

The evaluation focuses on execution accuracy, which is standard but incomplete. There is little analysis of SQL efficiency, robustness to database perturbations, semantic equivalence beyond benchmark answers, security/safety issues such as unsafe query generation, or failure cases where execution feedback is misleading.

Presentation is generally clear, but the manuscript has several polish issues: duplicated or confusing notation for turn count versus verification rounds, typographical errors, malformed table text from PDF extraction, inconsistent capitalization, and an example in Appendix H whose ordering appears internally inconsistent. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in careful reporting.

The ethics discussion is present but somewhat high level. For a system intended to let non-experts query real databases, the paper should discuss risks around privacy, access control, leakage through exploratory queries, and over-trust in plausible but wrong SQL outputs more concretely.
